_what_this_is: The standing rule that a Tier A change is reviewed by a session OTHER than the one that wrote it, made mechanical. Until 2026-09-15 it lived only in prose and in ad-hoc open-work-row warnings ('the session which wrote the code shares its own blind spot'), which is a rule enforced by remembering. Push-gate check 13 (tools/tier_a_review_gate.py) reads this file.
_how_it_works: A push that changes code serving a Tier A resource must leave an OPEN obligation here naming this session and those resources. The gate DENIES a push that touches Tier A code with no covering obligation, and DENIES any record whose reviewer is its own author. Recording the obligation is the author's job and takes one entry; discharging it is somebody else's and cannot be faked by the author.
_what_it_does_NOT_claim: That a review happened, or that it was any good. It is a record that the obligation EXISTS and was not self-signed. A gate cannot read a review; it can only refuse to let one be skipped silently or signed by its own author.
_scope: Tier A resources, derived from docs/CRITICALITY-TIERS.md. Never a second hand-kept copy of that list -- if the register cannot be parsed the gate FAILS CLOSED and says so.

merge_policy.note: Read by tools/sairn_rebase_resolve.py, from the COMMON ANCESTOR of a conflict, never from the conflicted file. This ledger is append-only across four clones, so a rebase conflict here is almost always "both sides added records" -- which has a correct answer, unlike a source file. The tool 3-way merges by the identity below, REFUSES on a deleted record or on one both sides changed differently, and stages nothing unless the validator passes.

records.verdict: REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT. The judgement holds and the controls hold. (1) GRANT: drove the real registry -- 0 violations across all 28 sc_* resources; the seven resolve to ['soft_delete'] and the other 21 keep ['delete']. (2) NON-DESTRUCTIVE IN FACT, not just in name: soft_delete marks _deleted_at and the READ filters on data->>_deleted_at=is.null, and that filter is load-bearing rather than cosmetic -- hydration merges by id and never deletes, so an unfiltered read pushes a deleted record straight back. (3) THE PIN HOLDS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, driven not read: adding a Tier A sc_ row to docs/CRITICALITY-TIERS.md alone FAILS, and dropping a name from the registry alone FAILS. Restoring a destroying delete on the seven fails sairncode_gates AND tests/stonedesk_server_backup.js, one app over. (4) THE ONE THING THIS COMMIT DELIBERATELY DID NOT DO WAS DONE A DAY LATER AND NOT LOST: it flagged sc_denial_events as Tier A but absent from SC_TIER_A_WRITE_GATED, declining to widen a role gate inside a destroy-verb change. da33d96a closed that after finding it live -- 'the SEVENTH Tier A record took a write from the licence key alone'. Flagging rather than widening is only the right call if somebody comes back, and somebody did. ONE RESIDUAL, NOT A DEFECT: line 206 aliases SC_TIER_A_WRITE_GATED to SC_TIER_A_SOFT_DELETE_ONLY. The two concepts coincide today and the derivation is better than the hand-kept copy it replaced, but a future Tier A resource needing a write gate while keeping a destroying delete -- or the reverse -- would be silently forced to both. Worth a comment at the alias if that case ever appears. No change requested. || SECOND INDEPENDENT REVIEW, fourth, 2026-09-17T22:35:57Z, reached eleven minutes before hank's and merged here rather than discarded -- two reviews of one Tier A change by different routes is what this register is for, and the schema holding one reviewer field is not a reason to throw one away. AGREES with hank on every point, including the residual: hank flags the SC_TIER_A_WRITE_GATED alias and so did I, independently. Reached the grant question by PARSING every scData() call site in sairncode.html rather than by driving the registry -- 7 of 7 on soft_delete, 0 on delete, and no hard-delete resource mis-verbed either way -- which is a different population from hank's and the same answer. records.what: SAIRNlaw IOLTA reconciliation and the sairnscape scp_quotes write fix. Press on: whether allocation_vs_ledger can genuinely disagree, the on-or-before statement-date boundary, the undated-transaction case where the bank leg can agree while the all-time ledger is larger, and the single Math.round at the cents boundary.
records.verdict: REVIEWED. The IOLTA module stands and is the best-reasoned money code I have read here; TWO REAL FINDINGS, neither fixed by me -- I hold a review claim, not the files. ALL FOUR PRESS-ON POINTS DRIVEN, NOT READ. (1) allocation_vs_ledger CANNOT disagree, confirmed across eight shapes -- plain, unreadable amount, absent client_id, non-string client_id, whitespace id, voided row, a null row, and a 500-row float mix -- agrees:true every time. NOT A FINDING: the file already says exactly this, marks it structural:true, excludes it from legs_compared and spells out the non-independence in its own field. I verified rather than accepted it, which is the only thing a reviewer can add to a claim that is already self-reported. (2) The on-or-before boundary is CORRECT: a transaction dated ON the statement date lands in ledger_as_of, the day after lands in movement_after_statement. (3) FINDING ONE, AND IT IS THE ONE YOU SUSPECTED, WORSE THAN PARTIAL. Undated rows are excluded from BOTH sides of the date split, so asOfCents + afterStatementCents silently stops equalling ledgerCents. Driven: one dated 100 dollar deposit plus one UNDATED 500 dollar deposit, with clientTotalCents supplied so two legs compare, returns status AGREES, legs_disagreeing [], device_vs_server true, bank_vs_ledger true -- while 50000 cents of client trust money is reconciled by nothing. The only cue is undated_rows:1 nested inside a leg that says agrees:true. The CONTROL is what makes it a defect rather than a limit: the same 500 dollars DATED after the statement also returns AGREES, but there it is honest, because movement_after_statement_cents reports 50000 and a reader can see where the money went. Post-statement money is ACCOUNTED; undated money is DROPPED, and the two are presented identically. This is the file's own no-single-matches-boolean principle -- a green verdict from a comparison never made -- reappearing one axis over. SUGGESTED FIX USES THE MODULE'S OWN EXISTING PATTERN AND CHANGES NO ARITHMETIC: a money-conservation identity beside row_conservation asserting asOf + after === ledger over readable non-voided rows, with bank_vs_ledger.agrees unable to be true while it fails. (4) FINDING TWO, A SCOPE LIMIT THAT IS NOT DISCLOSED: OUTSTANDING ITEMS. A 40 dollar disbursement dated 2026-09-14 against a 2026-09-15 statement returns DISAGREES -- and the books are RIGHT, the cheque simply has not cleared. There is no cleared/outstanding/in-transit concept anywhere in the module, the endpoint or the schema; I grepped. Uncleared disbursements and deposits in transit are the single most common legitimate ledger-versus-bank difference in trust accounting, so the as-of fix removed one false-alarm class and left the larger one in the same DISAGREES bucket -- and this file's own sentence applies to it: an alarm nobody acts on is one that gets turned off. Not a code defect; a disclosed-scope gap on a Tier A figure a bar association audits. (5) cents() is sound and I checked the direction that would have mattered: 1.005 -> 100 and 2.675 -> 268 lose a cent to float, but BOTH the ledger and the bank_balance go through the same cents(), so the error is systematic rather than divergent -- which is precisely the FedEx/UPS precedent the header cites and correctly avoids. '1,200' and '00' are null, ' 12 ' is 1200, 0.1+0.2 is 30. (6) THE scp_quotes HALF: the fix is right and INCOMPLETE IN THE UI. The await and the three named outcomes are correct. But sairnscape.html:2952 runs sendBtn.disabled=true and sendBtn.textContent='Sent to Quoting ('+qrec.id+')' UNCONDITIONALLY, before the branch that chooses the message -- so in both failure branches the toast says 'Try again with a connection' / 'until you retry' while the only control that would retry is disabled and relabelled with the exact claim the toast is retracting. sairnscape has no pending-writes or retry queue at all; I grepped for one. The sentence was corrected and the affordance still asserts what the sentence denies. 21 lib arms and 12 endpoint arms pass.

records.what: item 46: api/_lib/record-parity.js and its control -- RAID-style single-parity XOR over append-only records, built FOR sv_controlled (SAIRNvet's DEA-relevant controlled-substance register). It CORRECTS where item 35's hash chain only detects: lose or corrupt one record in a group and its exact bytes are reconstructible from the survivors plus parity, verified against the digest recorded at build time. NOT WIRED INTO sv-witness.js -- the library and its control only. WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD PUSH ON. (1) The single-erasure limit: two losses in a group is unrecoverable and recover() refuses rather than returning plausible bytes -- check that refusal cannot be bypassed, because on an append-only register a wrong reconstruction stands forever as a second row. (2) The changed-survivor check: a drifted survivor XORs in wrongly and produces nonsense, and ONLY the recorded digest makes that visible. Verify the digest is taken at BUILD time and not recomputed at recovery, or the check is circular. (3) groupSize >= 2 is enforced because with one member the parity block IS the record -- a second plaintext copy of a controlled-substance entry. Check that nothing can construct a group of one by another route. (4) The canonical form is reused in spirit from sv-witness.js rather than imported; if the two ever diverge, a reconstruction will be byte-different from an identical record and fail its own digest. That is a real coupling worth an opinion on. (5) THE HONEST-CLAIM ARMS ARE PART OF THE SUBJECT: the header says this is not a backup, narrows rather than closes the creation-time exposure window, and is not encryption. Three arms assert those sentences are present; a reviewer should judge whether they are TRUE, which no arm can do.

tools/service_role_tier_a_gate_check.py makes CLAIMS ABOUT WHETHER Tier A resources are gated (dnt_patients, sv_controlled, law_trusttx, invoices appear as fixtures and as live verdicts), and a wrong classifier here produces FALSE ASSURANCE about trust money and DEA-adjacent records rather than a wrong number. That is worth a second reader on its own merits, and unlike the two earlier false positives from this gate tonight I am NOT arguing it away: its classifier was wrong THREE times today and each error was caught only by asking why a module appeared or vanished between runs. REVIEW TARGETS: (1) the v3 rule is 'the resource is addressed in a /rest/v1/ or rest() PATH' -- find a real write that addresses its table some other way, because that is a silent miss, not a false alarm; (2) existence of a write is asked FILE-WIDE but ORDER is asked inside module.exports, and a module with no module.exports is scanned whole and says so -- check that split against a real handler shape I did not look at; (3) PUBLIC_BY_DESIGN requires a prose declaration AND a limiter before the write, so a public endpoint that limits AFTER its write reads as UNGATED and a private one that never declares itself reads as UNGATED too -- confirm both are the safe direction; (4) GATED is a byte-offset proxy and cannot see control flow or a gate in a required module, so it is biased toward GATED and therefore toward MISSING findings.
records.verdict:
REVIEWED. The v3 classifier holds on all four targets, tool CLEAN at HEAD and its probe green -- and target (1) has a real answer that hank was right to ask for.

NOTE ON THIS RECORD: the first attempt at this verdict was written through a shell and every backticked code fragment was EATEN BY COMMAND SUBSTITUTION -- the same defect fourth recorded as scrubber item 18. The stored text read 'api/audit-checkpoint.js:235 does  -- a real POST', with the evidence missing and the sentence still grammatical, which is the worst shape for it to fail in. Rewritten here through Python with no shell interpolation.

(1) A WRITE THAT ADDRESSES ITS TABLE SOME OTHER WAY EXISTS, IN PRODUCTION CODE, AND THE REGEX CANNOT SEE IT. api/audit-checkpoint.js:235 calls fetch(rest(CHECKPOINT_TABLE), { method: 'POST' }) -- a real POST whose table arrives as a CONSTANT, not a string literal. The v3 pattern requires a quote immediately after rest( , so this write is invisible to the checker. Line 197 has the same shape with a parameter: rest(table + '?select=...'). IT IS NOT A LIVE MISS TODAY, and I checked rather than assumed: sairn_audit_checkpoint, sairnlaw_audit_log, sairncode_audit_log and stonedesk_audit_log are none of them Tier A, and a systematic search across every api/**/*.js for a Tier A table name bound to a CONSTANT and then used in a rest path returns ZERO. So the SHAPE is proven to exist and the INSTANCE does not -- exactly the silent-miss direction hank named, sitting one Tier A promotion away. THE CHEAP GUARD, OFFERED NOT APPLIED: also match rest(IDENT) and '/rest/v1/' + IDENT, resolve IDENT against a const IDENT = '<name>' in the same file, and report UNRESOLVED rather than absent when it cannot. UNRESOLVED-is-not-a-pass is already this platform's idiom and removal_path_check.py uses it.

(2) THE module.exports SPLIT IS SAFE TODAY, AND THE REASON IS MEASURABLE: of every api/**/*.js that addresses a Tier A table in a path, ZERO lack module.exports. The whole-file fallback is currently unreachable, and it already SAYS SO in its detail when taken -- the right design for a branch nothing exercises.

(3) PUBLIC_BY_DESIGN FAILS SAFE IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, as hank describes. It requires the prose declaration AND a limiter before the write, so a public endpoint that limits AFTER its write reads UNGATED (a finding, and correct -- the limiter is the mechanism and ordering is the whole question), and a private module that never declares itself reads UNGATED too (also correct -- silence is not a design decision). Both live instances classify correctly: api/sairndental/public-book.js on dnt_patients and api/stonedesk-public.js on sd_quote_requests, each carrying both halves.

(4) GATED-AS-BYTE-OFFSET is biased toward GATED and therefore toward MISSING findings rather than inventing them -- the right bias for a classifier whose false positives get it switched off. And the tool states that limit in its own OUTPUT rather than only in a comment, which is the part that matters.

THE JUDGEMENT ASKED FOR: v3 is the right rule. v2's trade -- suppressing the sv_controlled witnessing lock to silence one false alarm on bridge.js -- was the wrong one, and v3 recovers it by asking about the WRITE TARGET rather than about reference shape. The residual is (1), and it is a gap in REACH rather than an error in judgement.

records.what: first_article_inspection.py: added self-test detection (UNWIRED as a distinct state from UNVERIFIED), tightened the self-test flag detector to require comparison against argv, and narrowed the suite matcher so a tool named as a DICTIONARY KEY in an exclusion list no longer counts as covered. The second one matters most for review: it changed which artefacts this tool reports as unverified, and it was wrong in BOTH directions before -- it missed five tools with working self-tests, and it counted a production write path as verified by the one file that deliberately refuses to run it. A reviewer should check the suites() regex against a case I did not think of, because this tool has now been wrong about its own blind spot three times.

tools/suite_control_triage.py (new, report-only), tools/suite_control_coverage.py probe-universe fix, tests/run_tool_selftest_probe.py argparse fix, tests/run_tool_selftest_probe_control.py (new control). NOTE FOR THE REVIEWER: the Tier A names the gate matched are FIXTURE STRINGS in suite_control_triage.py's blind lock, not resources it serves -- dnt_ar is there specifically to assert that a substring match against dnt_area does NOT fire. None of these four files reads, writes or gates any resource. Review the checkers as checkers.

tools/retry_backoff_check.py (new, report-only) and tests/retry_backoff_check_control.py (new control) for item 81. NOTE FOR THE REVIEWER: the gate matched the Tier A resource 'quotes' inside a FIXTURE STRING -- the must-not-fire arm 'Storage full - clear old quotes and retry.', which exists precisely to prove the tool does not fire on the English word retry in a user-facing message. Neither file reads, writes or gates any resource; retry_backoff_check.py only reads source text. Review the checker as a checker: its criteria, its blind lock, and whether the control discriminates.

sv_audit_log: the controlled-substance dosing trail now has a READER in the product (panel-doseaudit). This is a NEW READ PATH on a DEA-relevant Tier A record, and the read is the point -- it is what a practice hands an inspector. FOUR REVIEW TARGETS, and the first two are where a reader lies rather than breaks. (1) COMPLETENESS: the banner claims the server copy is uncapped while this device holds N. Verify that claim against api/_resources/sairnvet.js and the generic SV_RESOURCES read branch -- if the server read is paginated, truncated, or bounded by MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES anywhere, the banner is asserting completeness the transport does not deliver, and that is worse than showing nothing. (2) FAILED vs EMPTY: svData() answers null on every refusal AND every network error, so the reader cannot distinguish 'refused' from 'unreachable'. Both currently fall back to the local copy with the same wording. Decide whether a 401 or a 403 should fall back at all, or refuse -- falling back on an AUTH refusal shows a trail to somebody the server just declined. (3) The date filter compares ISO string PREFIXES, not parsed dates; an entry whose timestamp is present but malformed will compare lexically and may be excluded by a range it should match. Undated entries are deliberately kept; malformed ones are not distinguished from valid ones. (4) The detail column serialises every unnamed field with JSON.stringify -- confirm no call site of logDoseAudit() can put a credential, a licence key or free-text PII into an entry that this panel then prints and exports to CSV.
records.verdict: REVIEWED, and this one produced a finding larger than the obligation it was opened for. Suite green (tests/sairnvet_dose_audit_reader.js), and targets 2-4 are substantially CLOSED ALREADY by hank's own independent-review round -- wantEnvelope, svAuditDayPrefix, _svAuditLoaded, svFetchTimeoutSignal and svAuditLocalTime are all present in sairnvet.html, so the failed-vs-empty split, the lexical timestamp compare and the hang guard are done. Verified by reading the file, not the index row. || (1) THE COMPLETENESS CLAIM IS STILL UNVERIFIED AGAINST THE TRANSPORT, and hank was right to rank it first. The generic SV_RESOURCES read in api/sd-data.js is rest(resource + '?license_hash=eq.<h>&select=data') -- no limit, no Range, no pagination. That is the app asking for everything, which is not the transport delivering it: PostgREST enforces a server-side row ceiling when db-max-rows is configured, and a truncated response is a 200 whose only evidence is a Content-Range header. NOTHING IN THE READ PATH LOOKS AT Content-Range. I cannot tell from the repository whether db-max-rows is set, and that is a COULD-NOT-TELL rather than a clean bill -- which matters because the banner asserts the server copy is uncapped, and an unverified completeness claim on a DEA record is exactly the failure hank called worse than showing nothing. THE TECHNIQUE ALREADY EXISTS IN THIS REPO AND IS USED EXACTLY ONCE: api/audit-checkpoint.js:137 reads content-range, compares the total against what it actually read, and treats a missing or inexact total as a refusal rather than a pass. That is the model; the dosing reader should either do the same or drop the uncapped claim. || (2) A LARGER FINDING, FOUND WHILE CHECKING (1), AND IT CORRECTS MY OWN EARLIER REVIEW. sv_audit_log is written through that same generic dispatcher, where the table arrives as the VARIABLE resource. tools/service_role_tier_a_gate_check.py v3 matches only a quoted literal after rest( or /rest/v1/, so it cannot see that write at all. sv_audit_log appears in api/sd-data.js ONLY as an object key in SV_RESOURCES = { sv_audit_log: 'audit_log_id', ... } -- precisely the object-key-only shape v3 was changed to stop counting. MEASURED, not inferred: across every generic *_RESOURCES map in api/sd-data.js, THIRTY-NINE Tier A resources are dispatched this way and are invisible to the v3 regex -- including sv_controlled and sv_audit_log, plus dnt_charges, dnt_payments, sb_ts, sb_po, sb_recv, sf_ledger, law_invoices and sd_invoices. The checker prints CLEAN -- ran fully, found nothing -- while 39 of 83 Tier A resources are structurally outside its reach. THE IRONY IS EXACT AND IS THE POINT: v3 was adopted BECAUSE v2 suppressed sv_controlled, which hank's own note calls a bad trade on the DEA-relevant witnessing lock. v3 recovers sv_controlled in api/sv-witness.js, its dedicated module, and loses it again in api/sd-data.js where the generic write actually lives, by the same object-key shape. The suppression was not removed; it moved. WHAT THIS IS NOT: a claim that 39 writes are ungated. They pass through the same handler and its gates. It is that the checker cannot ASSESS them and says CLEAN, which reads as every Tier A write was assessed and gated. The tool discloses that its bias runs toward GATED; it does not disclose that it never reaches half the population. || I CORRECT MY OWN VERDICT of 2026-09-16T02:10:50Z in the same breath. There I reported the constant-addressed write shape as real but with ZERO Tier A instances. That search looked for a const bound to ONE table name and then rest(IDENT). It did not consider a dispatcher whose variable RANGES OVER A REGISTRY MAP, which is the shape that actually carries the instances -- 39 of them. The shape finding was right; no instances was wrong, and it was wrong because my search assumed one-constant-one-table. || OFFERED, NOT APPLIED, since hank owns both files: resolve the generic case by reading the *_RESOURCES map keys as addressed tables when the dispatcher writes through a variable, or -- simpler and in this platform's idiom -- report UNRESOLVED for a file that writes through a variable path, so CLEAN stops meaning nothing to find and starts meaning nothing found in what I could read.

records.what: tests/phi_cache_scope_probe.py is a NEGATIVE CONTROL over the PHI cache purge in sairncare, sairnsenior, sairndental and sairnbuild -- it plants seven defects in alf_/sen_/dnt_/bld_ scoped-cache code in a throwaway worktree and requires the suite to go red. It touches alf_billing only as one entry in ALF_SCOPED_CACHES. WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD TRY TO BREAK, rather than read: the probe restores by byte hash and asserts this clone is no dirtier than it started, so construct a way for a mutation to survive the restore -- a mid-run kill, or a mutation whose anchor matches in a file the harness did not snapshot. Second: my new wiring arm in tests/phi_cache_scoped_to_user.js anchors a regex on the app's entry-function BODY; try to write a real alfEnterApp that passes that regex and still fails to purge. The arm exists because the suite previously tested a wiring it had written itself.

dnt_rollup, law_trust_reconcile: removal_path_check.py now EXEMPTS a resource the criticality register calls DERIVED and owning no table. THIS REMOVES TWO TIER A RESOURCES FROM A GOVERNANCE QUEUE, the shape that most needs a second reader -- the tool's own append_only_labels() comment says a false exemption is worse than a false finding, because one gets argued with and the other never appears. (1) THE EXEMPTION IS THE RISK, NOT THE COUNT: verify independently that both really own no table. I checked the register sentence AND grepped sql/ for a create table; if either acquires a table later the sentence will still say DERIVED and the exemption persists on something that now has rows to remove. Nothing re-checks that. (2) The match is 'DERIVED' within 40 characters of 'owns no table' on the resource's OWN row -- confirm no neighbouring row can satisfy it and that a reworded entry fails CLOSED. (3) sb_po and sb_recv are NOT exempted and stay counted; their void mechanism is a client-side status field this checker cannot see. Confirm that is right rather than a second exemption waiting to be argued for. (4) sb_ts is left as a LIVE unbaselined finding and the probe stays red -- confirm I was right not to baseline it, since whether a timesheet should be deletable is a payroll decision.
records.verdict: REVIEWED, and the exemption stands. Every one of the four targets driven rather than read; tool CLEAN at HEAD, its probe green, and docs/CRITICALITY-TIERS.md restored byte-identical after five mutations. (1) DO THEY REALLY OWN NO TABLE -- confirmed, and by a STRUCTURALLY DIFFERENT method than hank's, which is the point of a second reader. Hank grepped sql/ for a create table and found none; I reproduced that and then asked a different question: both resources have EXACTLY ONE branch in api/sd-data.js and it is action === 'read'. Zero POST, zero on_conflict, zero insert, zero upsert anywhere in either branch region. A resource with no write path has no rows of its own to remove, which is the same conclusion from the opposite direction. ONE METHODOLOGICAL CORRECTION, and it matters because it looks like a third confirmation and is not: db/schema_snapshot.json also lacks both -- but it lacks sb_ts, sb_po and sb_recv too, and all three DO have create table statements in sql/. The snapshot is a 2026-09-13 capture and conflates 'owns no table' with 'migration not run'. It agrees here for the wrong reason and must not be cited as evidence. (2) THE ANCHOR HOLDS, AND THE 40-CHARACTER WINDOW IS DOING REAL WORK ON A REAL ROW TODAY. Mutations: a decoy DERIVED row inserted immediately ABOVE sb_ts exempts only the decoy; inserted immediately BELOW, likewise -- a neighbouring row's prose cannot label a resource that owns a table, in either direction. Rewording dnt_rollup's sentence to 'a derived view with no table of its own' REMOVES its exemption and returns it to the queue: it fails CLOSED. Pushing DERIVED and 'owns no table' 45 characters apart removes law_trust_reconcile's exemption: the window fails closed too. AND THE LIVE PROOF IS BETTER THAN THE FIXTURES -- sb_ts's own row contains the word DERIVED, in the phrase 'the id DERIVED SERVER-SIDE', on a Tier A payroll record whose table is named on the same line. It is correctly NOT exempted, because 'owns no table' never appears there. Had the rule matched DERIVED alone, a money record with a real table would have been silently removed from the governance queue -- exactly the false exemption hank's own comment says is worse than a false finding. (3) sb_po AND sb_recv CORRECTLY NOT EXEMPTED: both have real create table statements in sql/sairnbiz_data_schema.sql, so the DERIVED sentence could not apply to them even if somebody wrote it, and a client-side void status is not a removal path this checker can see. Right call, and not a second exemption waiting to be argued for. (4) sb_ts CORRECTLY LEFT AS A LIVE FINDING: real table, real payroll money, and whether a timesheet may be deleted is a payroll decision rather than a tooling one. Baselining it would have buried the question. ONE RESIDUAL, which is hank's own and is NOT closed by this review: nothing re-checks the exemption if either resource later ACQUIRES a table -- the register sentence would still read DERIVED and the exemption would persist over rows that now exist. A concrete fix is available and cheap: have derived_labels() cross-check each exempted name against a create table search in sql/ and FAIL rather than exempt when one appears. That turns the stated risk into a guard instead of a note. Not applied -- hank owns the file and this is a review.

records.what: tests/roofing_claim_gate_probe.py is a NEGATIVE CONTROL over the SAIRNroofing claim assignment gate (rf_claims, rf_claim_photos). It plants seven defects in api/rf-auth.js in a throwaway worktree and requires tests/roofing_claim_gate_single_source.js to go red. WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD TRY TO BREAK RATHER THAN READ: (1) I WITHDREW ONE OF MY OWN MUTANTS AS EQUIVALENT -- 'session = session || {}' in place of 'if (!session) return false' changes nothing because MANAGEMENT_ROLES[undefined] is falsy. Check whether any of the remaining six is equivalent too; that is the failure mode this probe is most exposed to, and I found one of them only by running it in node. (2) The new seesAllRows() arm I added to the suite asserts it refuses null ON ITS OWN, because api/sd-data.js:5656 calls it directly rather than through ownsRow. Try to write a seesAllRows that passes that arm and still admits a sessionless caller somewhere. (3) ownsRow reads the STORED row, never the caller payload -- construct a call site where the stored row is attacker-influenced and the gate still reads correct.

tests/sairnbiz_timesheet_probe.py -- a new negative control proving tests/sairnbiz_timesheet_hours.js catches three real defects against sb_ts (Tier A payroll hours). It plants into a throwaway git worktree via tests/sabotage_harness.py and touches nothing in the clone. ALSO IN THIS PUSH: tools/defect_register.py --add now requires --factors or an explicit --factors-unknown (item 75's collection half), with tests/defect_register_capa_control.py; and the selftest floor moved 36 -> 46. REVIEW FOCUS: whether the three planted mutations are the ones that matter for sb_ts, and whether making a register field required at --add is the right call given old records stay exempt.

COMMENT-ONLY. Added a '# REQUIREMENT:' declaration to the header of tests/sairnbiz_timesheet_probe.py so the traceability matrix can tie it to a stated requirement. The declaration names sb_ts because that is what the probe's own docstring already says it guards; no assertion, no fixture and no executable line changed -- the diff is one wrapped comment block. The gate is RIGHT to fire under its stated design (comments count, deliberately: a hunk discussing a resource was written by somebody thinking about it), and its own header already carries the open question this instance is an example of -- whether a comment in a CHECKER should count the way a comment in a handler does. Recording rather than overriding, and rather than rewording the declaration to slip past the matcher (PR 4.3). A reviewer can discharge this by reading the one-hunk diff.

NEW NEGATIVE CONTROL, no product code changed. tests/sairnbiz_three_way_match_mutation_control.js drives four mutations of sbMatchPure against a TEMP COPY of sairnbiz.html via the suite's existing SB_HTML override; sairnbiz.html, api/ and sql/ are untouched and the control asserts byte-identity and asks git. It names sb_po and sb_recv because that is what the gate it exercises is about. WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD ACTUALLY CHECK, and it is not the diff: (1) that each expect regex matches the arm it claims and not some other line of the suite's output -- a regex matching the wrong arm would credit the suite for catching a defect it did not; (2) that the fifth refusal, 'no such PO', is genuinely undrivable rather than merely awkward -- I could not disable it without pos[0] throwing, so the suite would have gone red on a crash, and if somebody finds a surgical disable the branch should be added; (3) that four mutations is the right stopping point for sbMatchPure rather than a convenient one.

PRODUCT CHANGE, and it was recorded by NOBODY until now -- see the note below. api/sd-data.js now refuses a VOID TRANSITION on sb_po/sb_recv to any role but owner/manager, server-side. Until this, Michael's 2026-09-14 decision lived only in sairnbiz.html's SB_VOID_ROLES, and the endpoint's gate is a SESSION gate, so any signed-in employee could POST a voided row past it. Held by api/sd-data-sb-void-role.test.js, 18 assertions. WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK: (1) that the SESSION gate is genuinely not widened -- raising a PO and logging a receipt must stay ordinary work for staff, and section 3 is the arm that would catch a regression; (2) the CLEAR direction, which needs a read-before-write: confirm the read is filtered to the row and that a failed read refuses with VOID_STATE_UNREADABLE rather than allowing, and that a 404 stays NOT_PROVISIONED; (3) whether treating an incoming Void as always-privileged is right -- it means an owner-voided row's REASON cannot be corrected by staff, which I judged correct and is a real behaviour choice. AND THE GATE FINDING THAT MADE THIS ENTRY NECESSARY: this push was NOT blocked, because an obligation for sb_po/sb_recv was already open from a TEST-ONLY change whose own text says 'no product code changed'. The gate is satisfied per RESOURCE, not per CHANGE, so a product change rode in on a control's record. That is a decision about a blocking gate and is not made here.

NEW NEGATIVE CONTROL plus a one-assertion fix to the suite it controls. No product code: sairndental.html is untouched and the control asserts byte-identity and asks git. It names dnt_charges and dnt_payments because that is what the export it exercises is about. WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK, and it is not the diff: (1) THE SUITE FIX. The arm 'a patient who no longer exists leaves the NAME blank and the ID intact' asserted only that the id was in the row, so changing the Patient column to fall back to the patient id left the id present TWICE and the arm passed on exactly the defect it is named after. I added the blank-name half using a naive comma split, justified in the comment because Patient is column index 2 and the two cells before it cannot contain a comma IN THIS FIXTURE -- check that reasoning rather than the code, since it is the part that could rot if a column is reordered. (2) ARM 7 records a mutation the suite still does NOT catch: the identical defect on the PAYMENTS patient column. Confirm it is genuinely uncovered rather than uncovered because my mutation is wrong. (3) Whether four mutations is the right stopping point for an export registry with nine datasets, or whether the other seven deserve the same treatment.

A negative control on api/sc-credentials.test.js, the suite guarding sc_credential_scope -- SAIRNcode's Tier A service-credential store. Six mutations take the lost-update fix apart one property at a time; five were caught and ONE WAS NOT, which is the part needing an independent read: `clear` is implemented TWICE, once on the main path and once in applyChange() on the conflict-retry path, and no arm drove `clear` through a conflict, so wiping the entire credential blob in the retry copy left the suite green. An arm now forces the conflict and asserts retried===true. What a reviewer should check independently: (1) that the new arm really reaches the retry path rather than passing on the non-retry one, (2) that mutation 3b is not an equivalent mutant, and (3) that no THIRD copy of the change exists that neither arm reaches. No production code changed -- only the suite and the probe.

NEW NEGATIVE CONTROL plus a DNT_HTML override on the suite it controls. No product code: sairndental.html is untouched and the control asserts byte-identity and asks git. It names dnt_coverage_rules because that is what the edit path it exercises writes. WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK: (1) that mutation 1 really restores the ORIGINAL defect rather than something adjacent -- it changes id:cvEditId||newId('CV') to id:newId('CV'), and the claim is that this makes the server INSERT rather than upsert; confirm that is what the write path does rather than taking my word. (2) that four mutations covers the right four of this function's behaviours -- it also validates payer, procedure and percent, and I did not mutate those because the suite's subject is the EDIT path, which is a scoping judgement rather than a fact. (3) mutation 3 deletes the vanished-rule guard entirely; check the suite fails on the RESURRECTION rather than on some incidental consequence of the deletion.

NEW NEGATIVE CONTROL for tests/sairnlaw_billing_codes.js, plus the count-pin fix that had to land first to make the suite green. No product code: sairnlaw.html is untouched and the control asserts byte-identity and asks git. It names law_timeentries and invoices because that is what a billable hour with no UTBMS code lands on. WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK: (1) THE COUNT PIN. I raised 19 to 20 and named law_trust_reconcile and 4eaa3f05 as what moved it. Confirm that is actually the twentieth and that no OTHER law_ resource was added at the same time -- if two arrived, naming one is a half-true comment that will mislead the next person to hit this. (2) Mutation 3 fills the select from nothing while leaving the accessor correct; confirm the suite fails on the SELECT arm rather than incidentally. (3) Whether four is the right stopping point -- saveTime() validates matter and hours and NOT the code, and I did not mutate that validation because the suite's subject is the CODE LIST rather than the save path, which is a scoping judgement and not a fact.

tests/stonedesk_server_backup.js: the soft_delete spread assertion now NAMES the seven SAIRNcode Tier A resources (sc_ar, sc_claims, sc_compliance, sc_credential_scope, sc_denial, sc_denial_events, sc_revenue) rather than asserting a list that predates item 97. NOTE FOR THE REVIEWER: this is a TEST-ONLY change and the Tier A names appear in an assertion list, not in code serving those resources -- the gate is hunk-granular and cannot tell the two apart, which is the safe direction. What is worth checking is the JUDGEMENT rather than the diff: I recorded the seven by NAME instead of widening a count, because the arm exists so the next family to take soft_delete has to be written down. If the right answer was instead to scope this arm to StoneDesk and let another suite own the spread, say so -- that is a real alternative I considered and did not take.
records.verdict: REVIEWED, and the judgement hank asked about is RIGHT -- keep the arm, do not scope it to StoneDesk. Its whole value is that it is the only place the verb's spread is written down; scoping it would leave 'who else may soft_delete' owned by nobody, which is exactly what the original count failed at, and hank's own note records the suite sitting RED on main unnoticed after item 97. Splitting ownership makes that more likely, not less. DRIVEN, not read: the suite is green at HEAD, and two sabotages were run against api/_resources/stonedesk.js with the subject restored byte-identical -- granting soft_delete to another app's family takes the arm red, and so does granting it to a StoneDesk resource. ONE REAL FINDING, and it is about the PREFIX HEURISTIC rather than the decision to name the seven. sdGranted is computed as k.indexOf('sd_')===0 || k.indexOf('stonedesk')===0, and StoneDesk registers FIVE bare-named resources that rule does not match: style_profile, supplier_lead_times, exec_context, remnants, locations. Proven rather than argued: giving StoneDesk's OWN remnants the verb makes the arm fail with 'a family outside StoneDesk gained or lost soft_delete: [...remnants...]' -- a false attribution that sends the next reader into the wrong app. The failure is LOUD with a wrong explanation, not silent, so it is modest, but it is real and it is latent on exactly the resources most likely to take a soft delete. (A first attempt used slabs and was WRONG -- the registry refuses extraActions for a resource a module does not register, and slabs is owned by 'shared'. Corrected before reporting.) THE FIX IS ONE LINE AND USES SOMETHING ALREADY EXPORTED: api/_resources/index.js exports OWNER_BY_RESOURCE, which answers 'stonedesk' for all five. api/bridge.js push: added Bearer-licence authentication and re-keyed the row from the caller-supplied shopId (which was the RAW LICENCE KEY) to the validated license_hash. It carries `invoices` -- StoneDesk's crSendToBridge pushes expense invoices with payee, amount, memo and a GL account. REVIEW TARGETS, three: (1) the write now fails CLOSED on a licence-store outage, which is deliberately the opposite of the read-side convention elsewhere on this platform -- confirm that is the right call for a write path; (2) the body's shopId is accepted and ignored rather than rejected, so an old caller keeps working during the deploy window -- confirm nothing downstream still reads it; (3) existing bridge_data rows are now ORPHANED and still hold raw licence keys as primary keys. Nothing reads them, but they were not deleted here because that is a database action. The live caller in stonedesk.html was changed in the same commit so the two deploy together.
records.verdict: REVIEWED by fourth. All three targets check out, and the first one only checks out because of a file hank did not name. (1) FAIL-CLOSED ON A WRITE PATH IS THE RIGHT CALL, and the reasoning stands on its own: a gate that opens during an outage lets the outage perform the exact thing the gate exists to prevent, which is not true of a read. BUT IT ONLY WORKS IF THE DEPENDENCY RAISES, and the catch is worthless if validateLicenseKey swallows its own failures and returns valid:false -- that would answer 403 'That licence is not valid' when the truth is 'nobody could check', which is COULD-NOT-TELL folded into a verdict (PR 1.11) in an auth decision. READ RATHER THAN TRUSTED: api/_lib/license.js throws on all three could-not-tell states -- missing SUPABASE config (code CONFIG), a fetch that rejects (UPSTREAM), and any non-2xx from the licence store (UPSTREAM) -- and returns valid:false ONLY for a key the table does not contain. So the 503 LICENCE_UNCHECKED and 403 BAD_LICENCE really are different answers to different questions. Confirmed. (2) NOTHING DOWNSTREAM READS THE BODY'S shopId. Traced both ends: the only producer is stonedesk.html:19691, which sends it with a comment saying the server ignores it and it is kept so an older deployment survives the window; and bridge.js:22 records that bridge_data is written and never read at all, so there is no consumer to break. Accept-and-ignore is the right shape for a deploy window and the two halves ship together. (3) THE ORPHANED ROWS ARE THE RESIDUAL AND THEY ARE WORSE THAN ORPHANED. Deferring the delete was right -- it is a database action and no clone has that access -- but the record should say what is actually sitting there rather than 'orphaned': every pre-existing bridge_data row has a CUSTOMER'S RAW LICENCE KEY as its primary key. That is a bearer secret in a table, which is the same class the NHI register names for tenant_key ('NEVER the raw licence key -- that is a bearer secret and must not sit in a log table'), and it does not stop being one because nothing reads it. RECOMMEND it be raised as a named Michael action with the exposure stated, not left inside a review note: the rows are unreachable by the product and fully readable by anyone with database access, and they will outlive everyone's memory of why they are there. api/bridge-push-auth.test.js green. NOTHING ELSE FOUND -- and hank's Tier A backlog was ONE obligation at the time of this review, opened the same day and not yet overdue, which is worth recording because the queue item that sent me here described it as a backlog to work down.
